text:
In the middle of a capacitive sensor characterization run, I noticed something wrong. The baseline was moving. Not in the expected way, not in the way the postdoc’s model predicted. The drift was systematic, it was correlated with the thing we were trying to measure, and it had been sitting in every prior measurement we’d treated as clean data.
That moment, staring at a trace that should have been flat but wasnt, is the reason this plan exists. Before it, I was the signal-chain guy building infrastructure for other people’s experiments. After it, I had a thesis.

title: Three Years to a Health Sensing Career
section: The Problem With the Default Path
text:
The Problem With the Default Path
My advisor’s lab is great at what it does. What it does is not Apple Health Sensing. The default trajectory is: build enough instrumentation, publish enough electrochemistry papers, graduate, maybe land somewhere adjacent. No one was going to stop me from drifting toward that default. I had to name the target explicitly.
Apple’s Health Sensing teams build the sensors in the Watch and AirPods. The MLIA team (Machine Learning Interpretability and Analytics) specifically looks for people who can find failure modes in sensing systems, characterize them rigorously, and design mitigations. That is my confound story, verbatim. The interview question is “walk me through a signal chain problem you solved end to end” and I already have the answer. I just need the papers to back it up.

title: Three Years to a Health Sensing Career
text:
The Three Phase Structure

Phase 0: Now to Aug 2026
August meeting with Ray. The key insight from talking to people who’ve pitched scientific pivots successfully: dont walk in proposing. Walk in with a one-pager that already has the problem statement, preliminary evidence, and a two-paper structure. The document does the convincing, not the conversation. If it doesnt exist yet, that is the actual work.
Syringe pump automation needs to finish because it is lab infrastructure cred. But I have to recognize it for what it is: zero signal to Apple. A clean GitHub portfolio with the DPV pipeline packages (dpv-monopeak, dpv-calibration) and the LSB205 voice-coil rig writeups is worth more than another conference poster. The data from the confound characterization runs goes in there.


Phase 1: Year 1
The confound characterization paper is the linchpin. No paper, no thesis arc. Target is a NeurIPS workshop on time-series for health (strong Apple recruiter presence) or EMBC. The Høst-Madsen ISIT paper needs to ship too, it is the strongest credential in the portfolio and proves I can do rigorous empirical ML outside my subfield.
Also start mapping Apple researchers. Ten specific names came up in the research: Salar Abbaspourazad, Joseph Futoma, Andrew Miller, Sinead Williamson, Nicholas Foti, Fahad Kamran, Jens Behrmann, Antoine Wehenkel, Guillermo Sapiro. Read their papers. Follow their work. These are the future interview committee.


Phase 2: Year 2
The fix-it paper showing the confound mitigation works. Needs to be submitted by early 2028 to be citable on an internship application. Target IEEE Sensors Letters for the faster review cycle.
The unified portfolio repo matters here. One clean artifact combining the rig characterization tooling and the DPV pipeline, with a README that tells the confound story end to end. An Apple engineer should be able to clone it, understand the problem, and see the evidence.
Internship applications open fall 2027. The checkpoint is non-negotiable regardless of how ready I feel.


Phase 3: Year 3
Interview prep. The confound story rehearsed as a narrative, not a results dump. Backup applications to Dexcom, Abbott, iRhythm in the same cycle, not after Apple rejects me. By the time you know Apple said no, the other cycles are closed too.

section: The Failure Points I Actually Worry About
text:
The Failure Points I Actually Worry About
Thesis arc drift. Ray’s lab has other priorities. If the confound work gets deprioritized for more instrumentation buildouts, I lose the differentiator. The checkpoint is concrete: if there is no first-author paper submitted by end of Year 1, that is a red flag, not ‘still early.’
Publishing in the wrong venues. A generic EE instrumentation paper with zero wearables framing does not read to Apple recruiters. Every title and abstract needs to be legible to a ‘wearable sensing’ search.
No internship means no shot. Apple’s research org almost never hires PhDs cold off a defense. If I miss the 2028 cycle, I am gambling on a second cycle in Year 4, which is late.
Becoming known for infrastructure, not insight. I am already the software and signal-chain guy in the lab. That is useful but it is a trap if it is all I am known for externally. The confound discovery is the thing that makes me a scientist instead of an engineer in recruiters’ eyes. Every paper, talk, and LinkedIn post needs to frame it that way.

This part is harder to write. Apple’s culture explicitly filters for people who can disagree without being disagreeable. Collaborative debate is the phrase they use. I have a pattern of being abrasive when I know I am right, and I have lost credibility because of it. The confound story only works if I can sell it, and selling it requires convincing skeptics without making them defensive.
Therapy is not separate from the career plan. It is part of it.

title: I Spent 15 Agents Investigating Whether My Lab Finding Is Actually a Hydration Sensor
text:
the gap is real. nobody has claimed it yet. the rest is work.
Two months ago I found a parasitic body-coupling capacitance term in the DPV sensor. The postdoc said it was drift in my measurement. It wasn’t. The body coupling was real, and getting rid of it became the thesis.
Then I had a stray thought: what if the parasitic term isn’t just a confound to kill. what if the residual signal, after mitigation, correlates with skin hydration state and is actually usable as a side-channel sensor.
Three claims chained together. characterize the parasitic term (in motion). apply mitigation (shielding, guarding, known technique). show the residual correlates with hydration (genuinely novel, if it holds). Each claim needs to survive independently. The third one is the bet.
This is the full audit. 15 research domains, ~120 papers, parallel agents running overnight. Everything I found about capacitive hydration sensing, skin dielectric physics, body capacitance biometrics, fringing-field design, the EDA differentiation problem, ground-truth reference methods, and the one gap that nobody has claimed.

title: I Spent 15 Agents Investigating Whether My Lab Finding Is Actually a Hydration Sensor
text:
The physics is solid, actually
Skin is a layered dielectric. Water dominates the permittivity. Gabriel et al. (1996, 3,000+ citations) established the canonical four-pole Cole-Cole model. Dry stratum corneum has ε_r ≈ 10 at 10 kHz. Hydrated SC hits ε_r ≈ 49. That’s a 5× swing in capacitance at wearable-relevant frequencies. The mechanism is lipid fluidization upon water uptake (Björklund et al., 2013 — parallel NMR/XRD confirmation). This is not speculative. It’s the physical foundation and it is settled.
The Yamamoto-Yamamoto finding (1976) that the SC has an exponential resistivity gradient (not a Cole-Cole arc) is the detail nobody in the wearable space cites but everyone should. The outermost layers dominate the measurement. This means a Corneometer reading at 1 MHz is a surface measurement, 10-20 µm deep into a SC layer that averages 15-20 µm. It reads the gradient’s surface, not the full water profile.
The SC swelling effect (Malnati et al., 2021 COMSOL model) is the gotcha. At high hydration, the SC thickens, pushing the fringing field away from the high-ε viable epidermis. Measured capacitance can paradoxically decrease. This is a genuine nonlinearity. Sensitivity is lower at high hydration. You can either curse it or model it. I’d recommend modeling it.

title: I Spent 15 Agents Investigating Whether My Lab Finding Is Actually a Hydration Sensor
section: The fringing-field geometry is a design constraint, not an open problem
text:
The fringing-field geometry is a design constraint, not an open problem
Penetration depth of interdigitated electrode fringing fields is proportional to spatial period λ = 2(W + G). Mamishev et al. (2004, Proc IEEE, 600+ citations) settled this. To target the SC (20-50 µm), you need W and G in the 30-100 µm range. That means reverse-offset printing (Dai et al., 2025, 50 µm gap) or microfabrication. Not standard screen printing, which bottoms out around 200 µm.
The Igreja & Dias conformal mapping model (2004, 260+ citations) gives you analytical closed-form capacitance for multilayer IDE structures. Pair that with COMSOL simulations parameterized with the Björklund skin dielectric values and you have a working sensor model with no experimental iteration needed. The sensor design is a solved problem. The interesting part is what you measure with it and how you separate the signal components.

title: I Spent 15 Agents Investigating Whether My Lab Finding Is Actually a Hydration Sensor
section: The EDA differentiation is faster to resolve than I expected
text:
The EDA differentiation is faster to resolve than I expected
I flagged this as homework in the roadmap: read the EDA/GSR literature to nail the mechanistic differentiation before drafting anything. Turns out the EDA community already did it for me.
Boucsein et al. (2012, “Publication Recommendations” — the EDA community’s own standardization paper) explicitly notes that lock-in amplifiers separate fast conductance (sweat duct ionic) from slow capacitance (SC hydration dielectric). The differentiation is baked into their own instrumentation recommendations. Martinsen & Grimnes (2001, “Facts and Myths”) is the canonical mechanistic paper: sweat ducts are conductive, SC moisture affects capacitive admittance. Bari et al. (2018) demonstrated empirically that SC (conductance), SP (potential), and SS (susceptance) have different morphologies when measured simultaneously.
The frequency argument is clean. EDA sensitivity peaks at ~100 Hz (Sridhar & Akl, 2017) because sweat duct ionic conduction dominates below 100 Hz. Above 1 kHz, dielectric polarization of bound water in the SC dominates. Operating a capacitive hydration sensor at 10 kHz-10 MHz is measuring a fundamentally different physical process. This is a one-paragraph differentiation in a paper, not a thesis chapter.
The reviewer question — “how is this not EDA with extra steps?” — has a short answer: conductance-based ionic vs. dielectric-based polarization, different frequency regimes, different physical pathways. The literature already supports it.

title: I Spent 15 Agents Investigating Whether My Lab Finding Is Actually a Hydration Sensor
section: The smoking gun: body capacitance is a biometric and it drifts
text:
The smoking gun: body capacitance is a biometric and it drifts
This is the finding that makes the hydration hypothesis more than a stray thought.
The human body acts as a floating conductor with body-to-ground capacitance C_B ranging from ~100 pF to several nF. It varies with posture, footwear, clothing, environment, proximity to objects. Aliau-Bonet & Pallàs-Areny (2012-2015) developed measurement methods for C_B across 10 kHz-1 MHz. Bian & Lukowicz (2019-2025) built systematic multi-factor studies of body capacitance for activity recognition.
The HCI community has been treating body capacitance as a deliberate signal for decades. Zimmerman’s three-mode body communication taxonomy (1995, CHI/IBM Systems Journal) is the foundation. DiamondTouch (Dietz & Leigh, UIST 2001) routed multi-user touch through individual body capacitance. PreTouch (Hinckley et al., CHI 2016) demonstrated that smartphone touch controllers can sense body proximity before contact — from a wrist form factor, same frequency regime, same hardware architecture as a hydration sensor.
And then there’s Platypus (Mujibiya et al., UIST 2011): person identification via body electric potential at 98.3% accuracy. A capacitive chair that can tell people apart just by the way their body capacitance loads the system. Twenty-two subjects, one second per measurement.
If body capacitance encodes enough person-specific information to serve as a 98.3% biometric, it plausibly encodes enough within-subject variation to track hydration changes. The day-to-day drift they observed could be hydration-related. Could also be clothing, sweat on the chair, environmental humidity. It is not demonstrated.
But the proof of concept — that body capacitance measured from a single contact point encodes fine-grained physiological state — is already published. EarFieldSensing (Matthies et al., CHI 2017) detected facial expressions from in-ear capacitive electrodes. CapSeat (Braun et al., CHI 2011) extracted posture from 16 car-seat capacitive electrodes. The hardware is the same. The signal extraction target is different.

title: I Spent 15 Agents Investigating Whether My Lab Finding Is Actually a Hydration Sensor
section: The touchscreen-to-hydration translation is already published
text:
The touchscreen-to-hydration translation is already published
Siyoucef et al. (2025, IEEE Sensors Journal) used an off-the-shelf TI FDC2114 module (28-bit LC-resonant capacitance-to-digital converter, 0.3 fF resolution) with a metallic plate as a finger-touch hydration sensor. 92% accuracy for athletes, 87% for fasting subjects, 4,000+ readings covering a 73-93% hydration range. KAUST lab, got picked up by New Atlas and EurekAlert.
An Apple Watch display is a capacitive touchscreen. If the touch controller can be repurposed for spot-check hydration — user touches the display for one second — no additional hardware. The FDC2214 is the exact IC family that shipped in smartphones for touch sensing. The Kim et al. (2020, Sensors) paper already demonstrated unmodified touchscreen panels detecting cardiac-synchronous finger capacitance changes.
Apple filed a patent in February 2024 describing dual-mode ECG/capacitive measurement circuitry reusing the Watch’s back-crystal electrodes. The patent describes: moistening an electrode surface, switching between ECG and capacitive measurement modes, using the same electrodes for both. Technically coherent. No shipping timeline. But the hardware architecture for capacitive hydration sensing from the wrist already exists in the Watch — it just needs the algorithm to extract hydration from the body capacitance signal component.
This is not a coincidence. It’s a verification that the question is well-posed.

title: I Spent 15 Agents Investigating Whether My Lab Finding Is Actually a Hydration Sensor
section: The ground-truth problem is circular and nobody talks about it
text:
The ground-truth problem is circular and nobody talks about it
Every wearable capacitive hydration sensor validates against the Corneometer CM825. This is a problem. The Corneometer operates at 0.9-1.2 MHz and measures dielectric permittivity — the same physical quantity as a capacitive hydration sensor. Correlation between two capacitance-based devices is expected by physics, not evidence of accuracy.
The actual gold standards: confocal Raman (direct water-to-protein ratio, 5 µm depth resolution) and NMR (direct proton density). Nobody in the capacitive hydration literature uses either. Fluhr et al.’s comparative study found a negative correlation (r = −0.45) between Corneometer and Raman total SC water AUC — capacitive sensors may be missing deeper SC hydration changes.
I have two options. Use Corneometer for initial validation to stay comparable with the literature, acknowledge the circularity, and call it correlation with the clinical standard rather than ground truth. Or seek Raman validation at IU dermatology as differentiating evidence for the NeurIPS workshop paper.
Leaning Corneometer first. If the data looks strong, Raman is the upgrade path. Don’t let the perfect reference block the initial measurement.

title: I Spent 15 Agents Investigating Whether My Lab Finding Is Actually a Hydration Sensor
section: LIG is the right research platform and nobody has used it for this
text:
LIG is the right research platform and nobody has used it for this
CO2 laser on polyimide at 10.6 µm. No cleanroom, no masks, no photoresist. Sub-$500 laser cutter. Sheet resistance as low as 9.5 Ω/sq. The Tour group at Rice established the fabrication baseline in 2014.
LIG interdigitated capacitive sensors exist for humidity (Paterakis et al., 2022 — 13,460 pF/%RH sensitivity, NFC wireless), aptasensing (Yagati et al., 2020 — 1.3 pM LOD in serum), and strain (Han et al., 2019 — GF ~0.47). Zero papers on on-skin hydration. Zero. The platform is established for three adjacent applications but the hydration angle is unexplored. Standard PI substrate, standard CO2 laser, standard IDC geometry — the sensor fabrication is a solved problem. The measurement and confound story is the novel part.
This also means LIG’s confound behavior is entirely uncharacterized: motion artifact, pressure variability, sweat interference, body capacitive coupling. All four of those confounds need to be studied systematically, and the cheap rapid-prototyping cycle of LIG (fabricate a new geometry in minutes, test on skin, iterate) makes it the ideal platform for that study. Even if the final product electrode technology ends up being something else, LIG lets you run the experimental design space before committing.

title: I Spent 15 Agents Investigating Whether My Lab Finding Is Actually a Hydration Sensor
section: The confound is studied in three communities and ignored in the one that matters
text:
The confound is studied in three communities and ignored in the one that matters
Body coupling capacitance C_B is:

The signal source in HCI/HBC research (Bian & Lukowicz, Grosse-Puppendahl, Zimmerman — treated as the carrier of useful information)
A quantified source of error in bioimpedance (Aliau-Bonet, IEEE TBME — causes “hook” artifacts and >137% measurement errors in tetrapolar BIA)
A target for active mitigation in touch sensing (TI CapTIvate, Cypress CapSense — active shielding, driven guard)
Completely absent from the capacitive hydration literature. Not a single published wearable capacitive hydration paper even mentions it.

The reason is straightforward. Every capacitive hydration paper validates in a controlled benchtop setup where the subject is seated, the sensor is taped in place with controlled pressure, and the measurement spot is on the volar forearm. C_B is held constant by experimental design. The confound is eliminated by protocol, not by measurement. It disappears from the data and therefore from the discussion.
On a moving wrist, under a watch strap with variable tension, with changing posture and proximity to grounded objects — C_B is large and time-varying and it swamps the sub-pF SC hydration signal. The fact that nobody has characterized this in a hydration context is not because it isn’t a problem. It’s because nobody has tried to make a wearable capacitive hydration sensor that actually works outside a benchtop.

title: I Spent 15 Agents Investigating Whether My Lab Finding Is Actually a Hydration Sensor
section: The mitigation toolbox exists, but it’s not a silver bullet
text:
The mitigation toolbox exists, but it’s not a silver bullet
Six technique families, ranging from standard (DRL, 70-123 dB CMRR, 50+ year legacy) to experimental (negative capacitance cancellation, 19.6 dB SNR improvement demonstrated, benchtop-only, stability issues).
The architecture that makes sense: active shielding (TI FDC1004 CapTIvate, protects the sub-pF signal path) + differential CDC (rejects near-field common-mode) + algorithmic compensation for the time-varying residual. Hardware alone won’t solve this because the confound itself is time-varying — posture, environment, strap tension all change C_B. Marcôndes et al. (2022) found that “no method seemed capable of mitigating the effects of electrodes’ capacitance that changes in the frequency spectrum.” The gap is algorithmic.
This is where the Apple Health Sensing MLIA team’s mandate — “analyze model behavior, identify weaknesses, lead investigations into failure modes” — maps directly onto the measurement problem. The confound is dynamic. Hardware can reduce it. ML can model what’s left.

title: I Spent 15 Agents Investigating Whether My Lab Finding Is Actually a Hydration Sensor
section: What’s actually novel vs. what’s established
text:
What’s actually novel vs. what’s established
Already settled, not my contribution:

Skin dielectric response to hydration (Gabriel 1996, Björklund 2013)
Fringing field penetration depth ∝ λ (Mamishev 2004)
LIG fabrication and humidity sensitivity (Tour 2014, Paterakis 2022)
EDA ≠ capacitive hydration (Martinsen/Grimnes 2001, Bari 2018, Boucsein 2012)
Body capacitance is a measurable physiological signal (Platypus 2011, Bian 2025)
Body coupling is a confound in bioimpedance (Aliau-Bonet, IEEE TBME)

Genuinely novel (nobody has published this):

Body capacitance as a hydration signal — nobody has proposed C_B as an indicator of skin hydration state
LIG capacitive sensor for on-skin hydration — zero papers
Body coupling confound characterization in the capacitive hydration context — the confound is well-studied in other fields but no capacitive hydration paper addresses it
The full three-claim chain (characterize confound → apply mitigation → residual signal correlates with hydration)
Touchscreen-to-wrist hydration translation for continuous wearable — Siyoucef 2025 did finger-touch, nobody has done continuous wrist

Three genuine gaps, not one. The characterization claim is novel within capacitive hydration (even though the confound physics is known elsewhere). The LIG-hydration pairing is novel. The residual-signal-as-hydration claim is novel. The chain is novel.

title: I Spent 15 Agents Investigating Whether My Lab Finding Is Actually a Hydration Sensor
section: The sweat-based commercial landscape is not competition
text:
The sweat-based commercial landscape is not competition
Three shipped hydration products as of mid-2026. All sweat-based. Gatorade Gx (microfluidic colorimetric, single-use, 16% failure rate). Epicore (electrochemical, FDA Class I, $32M Series B). Nix (electrochemical impedance, $129 DTC, no independent validation). BSX LVL Band raised $1.2M on Kickstarter, never validated the NIRS technology, refunded everyone, got acquired. Kenzen pivoted from consumer to industrial before shipping.
Zero capacitive hydration products exist. Zero. This means no commercial competition, but also zero commercial validation precedent.
The advantage of capacitive over sweat: no need for active sweating. Sweat patches require the subject to be sweating — they’re exercise-correlated, not continuous. Capacitive measures SC dielectric properties passively, continuously, regardless of sweat state. This is the pitch: hydration monitoring that works when you’re sitting still.

title: I Spent 15 Agents Investigating Whether My Lab Finding Is Actually a Hydration Sensor
section: Inter-subject variability means within-subject design is mandatory
text:
Inter-subject variability means within-subject design is mandatory
Pires et al. (2016, n=1,339) — only 18.23% of inter-subject SC moisture variance is explained by measurable demographics and environment. The remaining ~82% is unknown. Body site is the single largest variance source: SC thickness ranges from ~8 µm (abdomen) to 19 µm (forearm) to 100+ cell layers (palm). Men are ~6-7 AU drier than women. Age is non-monotonic (peaks ~40, then declines).
Within-person measurement CV is ~7.2%. Dry skin has higher variance. Probe pressure alone causes 40% variance in dry skin Corneometer readings — on a wearable with uncontrolled strap tension, this is squared.
The study design conclusion: within-subject crossover (each person is their own control), N = 20-50, 3-5 repeated measures per condition, baseline after 20-30 min acclimation, primary endpoint is percentage change from baseline not absolute capacitance. Universal calibration across subjects is not supported by any evidence. Don’t try it.

text:
2 Signal Processing Background
The raw accelerometer output is a time series sampled at 256 Hz, recorded in \(g\) (gravitational units). The first step is unit conversion to m/s^2 by multiplying by 9.80665. From there, the Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) is computed via FFT to obtain the frequency content of each segment.
The DFT of a length-\(N\) signal \(x[n]\) is:
\[X[k] = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x[n] \cdot e^{-j2\pi kn/N}\]
The corresponding frequency bins are spaced by the bin width:
\[\Delta f = \frac{f_s}{N}\]
At \(f_s = 256\) Hz, frequency resolution depends on segment length. Shorter station runs produce coarser bins. The one-sided amplitude spectrum (positive frequencies only) is used, with interior bins scaled by \(\sqrt{2}\) to account for the energy in the discarded negative-frequency half of the two-sided spectrum.

title: Ride Quality Analysis of a Passenger Rail System
text:
3 1/3 Octave Band Analysis
ISO 2631-1 specifies comfort limits at 1/3 octave band center frequencies, which are tabulated in the standard. Rather than applying a rectangular window over each band, a smooth bandpass gain function is applied at each FFT bin. This follows the fractional octave spectra method described by Audio Precision [2], using a 6th-order Butterworth-style gain centered on the upper edge frequency \(f_m\) of each band:
\[g_n = \sqrt{\frac{1}{1 + \left[\left(\frac{f}{f_m} - \frac{f_m}{f}\right) \cdot 1.507 \cdot b\right]^6}}\]
where \(b = 3\) for 1/3 octave bands. The gain is zero far from the band center and peaks at the center frequency, giving a smooth bandpass response that avoids the spectral leakage artifacts of a hard rectangular window.
The RMS value for each band \(L_b\) is:
\[L_b = \sqrt{\sum_{n=1}^{N} (F_n \cdot g_n)^2}\]
where \(F_n\) is the one-sided amplitude at frequency bin \(f_n\). This value is plotted at the upper edge of each 1/3 octave band and compared against the ISO comfort curves.

text:
4 Core DSP: compute_octave_rms
This function is the core of the pipeline. Given a raw acceleration segment in \(g\), it returns a 20-element array of RMS values, one per 1/3 octave band, ready to be plotted against the ISO limits.
A few implementation notes. The interp1d call allows the spectrum to be evaluated at arbitrary frequencies rather than only at FFT bin edges. This matters at short segment lengths where bin spacing is coarse and some narrow bands may fall between bins entirely. The floor clamp at 0.009 m/s^2 is a display artifact that keeps the log-scale axes clean when a band has essentially zero energy; it has no effect on the ISO comparison. The \(\sqrt{2}\) one-sided scaling is addressed in detail in Section 9.

def compute_octave_rms(segment_g):
    """
    Compute 1/3 octave band RMS spectrum from a raw accelerometer segment.

    Parameters
    ----------
    segment_g : np.ndarray
        Raw accelerometer values in g, sampled at 256 Hz.

    Returns
    -------
    list
        RMS magnitude (m/s^2) for each of the 20 1/3 octave bands.
    """
    fs = 256  # Hz
    N  = len(segment_g)

    # Convert g to m/s^2
    y = segment_g * 9.80665

    # FFT, normalized two-sided amplitude spectrum
    yf = fft(y)
    P2 = np.abs(yf / N)

    # One-sided spectrum: [0, N/2], scale interior bins by sqrt(2)
    P1 = P2[:int(np.floor(N / 2))]
    f  = np.arange(0, fs / 2, fs / N)

    # Edge case: length mismatch at odd N
    if len(f) > len(P1):
        P1 = P2[:int(np.floor(N / 2)) + 1]

    P1[1:-2] = np.sqrt(2) * P1[1:-2]

    # Interpolator to evaluate spectrum at arbitrary frequencies
    f_interp = interpolate.interp1d(f, P1)

    rms_per_band = []
    for v in range(len(higherBand) - 1):
        f_bins = f[np.where(np.logical_and(f >= centerF[v], f < centerF[v + 1]))]

        L = 0.0
        for x in f_bins:
            # 6th-order Butterworth bandpass gain per Audio Precision method
            gnb = np.sqrt(1 / (1 + np.power(((x / higherBand[v] - higherBand[v] / x) * 1.507 * 3), 6)))
            F_n = float(f_interp(x))
            L  += (F_n * gnb) ** 2

        L = np.sqrt(L)
        L = max(L, 0.009)  # display floor
        rms_per_band.append(L)

    return rms_per_band

6 Data Ingestion and Segmentation
Each accelerometer CSV contains a device metadata header spanning the first 21 rows, followed by the time-series samples. Station departure and arrival row indices are embedded directly in the CSV alongside the acceleration data, so segmenting by station requires no external lookup table. Columns 3 and 4 (zero-indexed) carry the lateral and vertical channels respectively, column 5 carries arrival row indices, and column 6 carries departure row indices.
Each file corresponds to one train run. Multiple runs are loaded together and overlaid on the same plot per segment to compare trains and identify outliers.

    print(" ", t)


def load_run(filepath):
    """
    Load one accelerometer CSV.
    Returns lateral signal, vertical signal, and depart/arrive row index lists.
    """
    df = pd.read_csv(filepath, sep=',', dtype='unicode')
    df = df.iloc[21:-1, :].reset_index(drop=True)

    depart_rows = df.iloc[0:16, 6].values.tolist()
    arrive_rows = df.iloc[1:17, 5].values.tolist()

    lat  = df.iloc[:, 3].astype(float).to_numpy()
    vert = df.iloc[:, 4].astype(float).to_numpy()

    return lat, vert, depart_rows, arrive_rows


def load_directory(data_dir):
    """
    Load all CSV runs from a directory.
    Returns parallel lists of labels, lat signals, vert signals, and depart/arrive matrices.
    Matrices are transposed so indexing is [segment][run].
    """
    labels, lat_matrix, vert_matrix = [], [], []
    depart_matrix, arrive_matrix = [], []

    for fname in sorted(os.listdir(data_dir)):
        fpath = os.path.join(data_dir, fname)
        if not os.path.isfile(fpath):
            continue
        lat, vert, departs, arrives = load_run(fpath)
        labels.append(os.path.splitext(fname)[0])
        lat_matrix.append(lat)
        vert_matrix.append(vert)
        depart_matrix.append(departs)
        arrive_matrix.append(arrives)

    depart_matrix = np.array(depart_matrix).T.tolist()
    arrive_matrix = np.array(arrive_matrix).T.tolist()

    return labels, lat_matrix, vert_matrix, depart_matrix, arrive_matrix

7 Synthetic Validation Dataset
To validate the pipeline end-to-end without the original accelerometer files, synthetic signals are generated with known frequency content. A realistic rail vibration signal has dominant energy in the 1 to 10 Hz range from suspension dynamics, with decaying higher-frequency content from wheel-rail interaction. Sinusoidal tones are injected at known ISO 2631-1 center frequencies so their presence in the correct octave bands can be verified in the output.

np.random.seed(42)
fs       = 256
duration = 60
t        = np.arange(0, duration, 1 / fs)
N        = len(t)

# Broadband colored noise base: pink-ish spectrum decaying with frequency
freqs = np.fft.rfftfreq(N, 1/fs)
freqs[0] = 1  # avoid divide by zero at DC
pink_spectrum = 1 / np.sqrt(freqs)
pink_spectrum[0] = 0

def colored_noise(scale):
    phases = np.random.uniform(0, 2 * np.pi, len(pink_spectrum))
    spectrum = pink_spectrum * np.exp(1j * phases)
    return np.real(np.fft.irfft(spectrum, n=N)) * scale

# Lateral: pink noise base + tones at ISO center frequencies
lat_synthetic = (
    colored_noise(0.004)                          +
    0.008 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 2.0  * t)         +
    0.005 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 3.15 * t)         +
    0.004 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 5.0  * t)         +
    0.002 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 8.0  * t)         +
    0.001 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 12.5 * t)
)

8 Plotting Against ISO 2631-1 Comfort Limits
The ISO 2631-1:1985 comfort limits are piecewise-linear in log-log space. The lateral and vertical axes have different curves, reflecting that humans are more sensitive to vertical vibration in the 4 to 8 Hz range, which corresponds to the resonant frequency of the seated human torso. Both limits are overlaid as dashed red lines. Any run with points above the red line is exceeding the comfort standard for that segment and frequency band.
The limit curve coordinates are digitized from the 1-hour reduced comfort boundaries in ISO 2631-1:1985 [1]:

Lateral: flat at approximately 0.27 m/s^2 from 1 to 2 Hz, rising above 2.5 Hz
Vertical: most restrictive in the 4 to 8 Hz range, rising above 8 Hz


def plot_rqa_segment(lat_segments, vert_segments, labels, title, markers=None):
    """
    Plot lateral and vertical 1/3 octave RMS spectra for one station segment
    with ISO 2631-1 comfort limit overlays.

    Parameters
    ----------
    lat_segments  : list of np.ndarray
    vert_segments : list of np.ndarray
    labels        : list of str
    title         : str
    """
    default_markers = ["o", "v", "^", "<", ">", "X", "1", "2", "3", "4", ","]
    if markers is None:
        markers = default_markers

    # ISO 2631-1 limit curves digitized from standard
    lat_lim_x  = [1, 2, 2.5, 80]
    lat_lim_y  = [0.85/3.15, 0.85/3.15, 1.06/3.15, 33.5/3.15]
    vert_lim_x = [1, 4, 8, 80]
    vert_lim_y = [2.36/3.15, 1.18/3.15, 1.18/3.15, 11.8/3.15]
    y_ticks    = [0.01, 0.0315, 0.1, 0.315, 1, 3.15, 10]

    fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(8.5, 11), sharex=False, dpi=150)
    fig.tight_layout(pad=5.0)

    for ax, segments, lim_x, lim_y, axis_label in [
        (ax1, lat_segments,  lat_lim_x,  lat_lim_y,  "Lateral"),
        (ax2, vert_segments, vert_lim_x, vert_lim_y, "Vertical")
    ]:
        for i, seg in enumerate(segments):
            rms = compute_octave_rms(seg)
            ax.scatter(higherBand[:-1], rms, marker=markers[i % len(markers)], label=labels[i])

        ax.plot(lim_x, lim_y, linestyle='dashed', color='red', label='ISO 2631-1 limit')
        ax.set_xlim(1, 80)
        ax.set_xscale('log')
        ax.set_yscale('log')
        ax.set_ylim(0.009, 10)
        ax.set_yticks(y_ticks, y_ticks)
        ax.set_xticks(centerF[:-1], centerF[:-1], rotation=45)

            ax.legend(loc='upper left')

text:
9 FFT Magnitude Scaling
The hardest part of building this pipeline was not the 1/3 octave filter math; it was getting the FFT magnitude scaling right.
The FFT of a real signal produces a two-sided spectrum where positive and negative frequencies each carry half the energy of the original sinusoid. When folding to a one-sided spectrum, the energy in the discarded negative-frequency half must be restored by multiplying interior bin amplitudes by \(\sqrt{2}\). The DC bin (\(k = 0\)) and the Nyquist bin (\(k = N/2\)) are not doubled since they have no negative-frequency counterpart.
The normalization that produces correct results is:
\[P_1[k] = \sqrt{2} \cdot \frac{|X[k]|}{N}, \quad k \in (0,\, N/2)\]
with endpoints left unscaled. Getting this wrong produces output with the correct spectral shape but a consistent vertical offset on every band. The frequency-domain structure looks right, but every RMS value is off by the same factor. Once you have a reference dataset to compare against, the diagnosis is straightforward: a systematic magnitude offset with perfectly matching trends is a scaling error.
Without the \(\sqrt{2}\) correction, the FFT underestimates the true amplitude by a factor of \(\sqrt{2}\). With the correction applied, the peak lands exactly at the expected value.

text:
10 Full Pipeline
The complete pipeline wraps all of the above: given a directory of CSV files, it loads all runs, slices each by station segment using the embedded row indices, and produces one figure per segment with all runs overlaid.

def run_rqa(data_dir, output_dir, start_seg=0, end_seg=16):
    """
    Full RQA pipeline: load all runs in data_dir, compute 1/3 octave spectra
    per station segment, and save one PDF per segment to output_dir.

    Parameters
    ----------
    data_dir   : str   directory of accelerometer CSV files
    output_dir : str   directory to write output PDFs
    start_seg  : int   first segment index (inclusive, 0-indexed)
    end_seg    : int   last segment index (exclusive)
    """
    os.makedirs(output_dir, exist_ok=True)
    matplotlib.use('Agg')

    labels, lat_matrix, vert_matrix, depart_matrix, arrive_matrix = load_directory(data_dir)
    markers = ["o", "v", "^", "<", ">", "X", "1", "2", "3", "4", ","]

    for seg_idx in range(start_seg, end_seg):
        title = segment_titles[seg_idx]

        lat_segs = [
            lat_matrix[run][int(depart_matrix[seg_idx][run]):int(arrive_matrix[seg_idx][run])]
            for run in range(len(labels))
        ]
        vert_segs = [
            vert_matrix[run][int(depart_matrix[seg_idx][run]):int(arrive_matrix[seg_idx][run])]
            for run in range(len(labels))
        ]

        fig = plot_rqa_segment(lat_segs, vert_segs, labels, title, markers)
        out_path = os.path.join(output_dir, f"{title}.pdf")
        fig.savefig(out_path)
        plt.close(fig)
        print(f"Saved: {out_path}")

title: Experiment Platform
text:
We needed to characterize capacitive sensors under mechanical load. The question is simple: how does capacitance track applied force across different drive frequencies and probe configurations? Running this by hand means one person at the bench for hours, adjusting brackets, watching an oscilloscope, writing numbers in a notebook, and inevitably missing something. The experiment platform replaces all of that with a script.
Three instruments are involved. An LCR meter measures capacitance and parallel resistance over serial. A Vernier GoDirect force gauge measures force over USB at up to 1000 Hz. An Arduino Mega drives a cam against the sensor via PWM. The platform orchestrates all three, logs everything to CSV, and runs two experiment types: a static LCR frequency sweep and a dynamic actuator experiment where the cam oscillates at controlled frequencies while capacitance and force are recorded simultaneously.

title: Experiment Platform
text:
Two layers, one threading core
The platform has two entry points that share the same concurrency model. cli.py is the interactive bench runner. It prompts for a box label and sensor index, offers LCR static, actuator sweep, or both, and loops over sensors with human-in-the-loop bracket selection and retry prompts. This is what a researcher uses at the bench.
run_headless.py is the autonomous optimization layer. It reuses the same ForceState, threading functions, and CSV writing from actuator.py, but strips out every interactive prompt. The loop decides its own next move by reading metrics from score_run.py, a frozen ruler that computes SNR, drift-corrected contrasts, and noise floor from the CSVs a run produces. The knobs it tunes are LCR probe frequency and aperture. The goal is maximizing signal-to-noise without a human in the loop.
Both layers share a single config.py file as the source of truth for all parameters: sweep frequencies, mechanical frequencies, bracket positions, servo gains, hardware ports, output directories. No hardcoded values anywhere else. A researcher edits one file. The loop edits the probe frequency and aperture fields. Everything else is read-only.

title: Experiment Platform
text:
The threading model
The actuator experiment runs three concurrent flows and one shared mutable object. The shared object is ForceState, a lock-guarded cell holding the latest force reading and its timestamp. That is the only mutable state shared between threads.
The force thread steps the frequency controller at the GoDirect sensor rate, publishing force to ForceState on every sample. The LCR thread measures capacitance as fast as the meter allows, which is about 40 Hz — the hardware bound, not a code limit. Each LCR measurement grabs the latest force from ForceState under lock and pushes a complete row to a queue. The main thread drains the queue to CSV.
This design means force and capacitance are never perfectly synchronized. The LCR meter takes 25 to 40 milliseconds per measurement. By the time it returns, the force gauge has produced several new readings. The row written to CSV includes force_age_ms: the difference between the LCR timestamp and the force timestamp. This column is the whole sync diagnostic. If force_age_ms is large and variable within a run, the lock contention pattern is wrong or the LCR meter is unusually slow. If it is small and stable, the two sensors are effectively synchronized at the timescale that matters.

title: Experiment Platform
text:
Stabilization before recording
Before recording begins at a target mechanical frequency, the force thread runs alone in a stabilization phase. The main thread polls FrequencyController.last_hz until it lands within the configured tolerance of the target, or times out. This is not a tight control loop. The controller updates last_hz every five seconds by counting force peaks. The stabilization loop accounts for this lag: it does not expect instantaneous convergence.
If stabilization times out, the frequency is skipped with a log message. Nothing crashes. The experiment moves to the next bracket or frequency. This is designed for unattended runs that might hit a loose bracket or a sensor that shifted during an earlier frequency step. The data from that step is lost, but the run continues.

title: Experiment Platform
text:
Interleaved variant
The optimization loop uses a variant called interleaved mode. Instead of recording one LCR probe config per run, it walks a schedule of config blocks within a single continuous strike train. Each block switches the LCR probe frequency and aperture, tags every row with config_id and block_index, and runs for a fixed number of mechanical cycles rather than a fixed number of seconds. The force thread runs continuously across all blocks, so every config sees the same sensor state scattered across the drift direction.
The scorer then fits drift out as a nuisance covariate. Drift-corrected SNR lets the loop compare configs that were measured seconds apart on a sensor that might be warming up, settling, or degrading. Without this, the loop would mistake drift for a better probe setting and optimize toward whatever config happened to run last.

title: Experiment Platform
text:
The quality heuristic
The LCR static sweep includes a sensor quality check called _is_clean. Six checks, empirically tuned for the specific capacitive sensor under test. Rejects negative capacitance, coefficient of variation above 0.20, monotonicity violations, outlier jumps, and end-point degradation below fifty percent of the initial value. If a sweep fails, the researcher is prompted to re-run or discard.
This heuristic is the kind of thing that sounds subjective until you watch someone spend twenty minutes analyzing data from a sensor that was dead before the experiment started. The check catches the obvious failures before they reach analysis. The thresholds are editable in one place. If a sensor type needs different criteria, change the numbers.

title: Experiment Platform
section: Safety and what it does not cover
text:
Safety and what it does not cover
The killswitch subsystem watches a flag file at the repo root. If a file named STOP appears, the headless runner zeros PWM on the live Arduino handle and aborts. A standalone command, killswitch.py stop, writes the flag and tries to open the Arduino port to force PWM zero directly.
Here is the gap. On Windows, COM ports are exclusive. If the runner holds ARDUINO_PORT, the standalone stop command cannot open it. The safety depends on the runner process being alive and scheduling threads to poll the flag file. A wedged process, a USB hang, or kill -9 bypasses the watcher entirely. The code is explicit about this. There is no firmware dead-man switch. Do not run the loop fully unattended.
A second runtime guard watches peak-to-trough force over a five-second sliding window. If the swing drops below a configurable threshold mid-run, the cam has stalled or the tape loosened, and the run aborts with a non-zero exit code. Running the optimization loop against a mechanically dead rig would produce garbage metrics, and the loop would tune toward whatever random noise the LCR meter picked up.

title: Experiment Platform
text:
The import shim
All three roots — repo root, system_code/, optimization_project/ — are on sys.path via a venv .pth file. Every module imports flat: from config import ..., from killswitch import ..., no package-qualified imports like system_code.experiments.actuator. The .pth file is not checked in because .venv/ is gitignored. A fresh checkout must recreate it before anything runs.
This is ugly. The alternative is proper package layout with namespace packages and pip install -e ., but that would add setup overhead and break the existing import chains that the actuator platform upstream already depends on. The shim is a deliberate tradeoff: ugly but zero-friction for the workflows that exist.

title: Experiment Platform
text:
What I would change
The two-layer split between system_code/ and optimization_project/ happened incrementally. The interactive platform came first. When I needed a headless loop, I added a new directory and imported threading functions from the interactive code by flattening the import paths. This works but it means the threading core lives inside actuator.py, which is also the interactive experiment runner. If I were starting over, the threading model would be its own module that both entry points import from, and actuator.py would be thin orchestration plus the interactive prompt loop.
The import shim would also go away. Proper package structure from the start would have saved the .pth hack and the mental overhead of explaining it in the architecture doc.
But both of those are about cleanliness, not correctness. The rig runs. The data is good. The optimization loop converges. The sync diagnostic (force_age_ms) proved that the threading model works at the timescale that matters. Everything after that is refactoring.

title: dpv-monopeak
text:
I kept rewriting the same peak-extraction code across calibration experiments. Find the max, subtract a baseline, pull some slopes off the shape. Every notebook had its own version, each broken in its own special way. The third time I tracked down a sign error in a width calculation, I gave up and made it a library.
dpv-monopeak does one thing. You hand it a voltage array and a current array from a Differential Pulse Voltammetry scan with a single dominant Faradaic peak. It hands back eight electrochemical features and every intermediate it used to get them. That is the whole scope.

title: dpv-monopeak
text:
The monopeak assumption
The name is the constraint. One Faradaic peak per scan, no more. If your voltammogram has multiple redox couples, the global current maximum wins and everything else is treated as background. No peak fitting, no deconvolution.
That looks like a limitation. It is the point. Multi-peak DPV is a different problem with different failure modes and a baseline model that is far more involved. Refusing to handle it keeps this library small enough to read in one sitting and fast enough to run on thousands of scans without anyone wondering what is happening inside.

title: dpv-monopeak
section: The baseline and the capacitive hump

title: dpv-monopeak
text:
The eight features
Once the anchors are placed, the rest is deterministic geometry. The baseline is a straight line between the left and right current minima flanking the peak. The corrected current is i - baseline. From there:
X is the peak voltage, the voltage at the maximum of the corrected current. This is your redox potential proxy, the primary signal of which analyte you are looking at.
Height is the peak current after baseline subtraction. It scales with concentration and it is the most direct quantitative feature.
Area is the trapezoidal integral of the corrected peak between the anchors. It holds up better than Height when the peak shape shifts across replicates.
Width is the FWHM, the voltage span at half the peak height. It needs both half-max crossings to exist and returns NaN if one is missing, which is more honest than guessing.
YOffset is the baseline current at the peak voltage, the non-Faradaic background. If this drifts across a concentration series while Height stays flat, your electrode is fouling rather than the analyte changing.
MaxSlope and MinSlope are the steepest rising and falling slopes of the corrected peak, computed as finite differences on the raw data with no smoothing. Positive and negative by convention. Sharp peaks get large absolute values, broad peaks get small ones.
SumSlope is MaxSlope + abs(MinSlope), a single number for peak sharpness. Narrow, well-defined peaks score high. Broad, flat peaks score low.
Every one of these has a physical meaning. None of them are dimensionless scores or model embeddings. They are numbers you can point at on the voltammogram and explain to a colleague in one sentence.

title: dpv-monopeak
text:
When it returns None
The extraction returns None when the scan does not contain a valid single peak. Arrays of different lengths, fewer than five points, flat current, duplicate voltage values, a peak sitting at either edge of the window, a positive peak height (which would put the baseline above the peak, impossible for a real Faradaic signal), zero peak area. Each gets its own early return with no diagnostic message.
That is deliberate. The calling code loops over hundreds of scan files. When a scan fails, the loop skips it and logs the filename. A detailed error per scan would bury the researcher in noise. The failure is the signal: this scan has no valid monopeak, move on.

title: dpv-monopeak
text:
Two functions, not one class
Two public functions, no classes. extract_dpv_features returns the eight features as a flat dict. compute_dpv returns those eight plus every intermediate: the baseline array, the corrected current, the half-max indices, the derivative array, the slope indices. Use extract_dpv_features for batch processing and compute_dpv when you need to plot a result or debug a scan that is misbehaving.
They share internals. extract_dpv_features calls compute_dpv and drops the extra keys. No duplication, and no way for the two paths to drift apart.
from dpv_monopeak import extract_dpv_features

v = df["v_V"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
i = df["i_uA"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
feats = extract_dpv_features(v, i)
if feats:
    print(f"{feats['X']:.4f} V, {feats['Height']:.2f} uA")

title: dpv-monopeak
text:
Plot as sanity check
The optional plot_dpv function gives you a two-panel figure: raw current with baseline on top, corrected current with FWHM and area shading on the bottom. It takes the same left_chop_fn parameter, so the plot matches whatever extraction logic you are running. It is the fastest way to confirm the baseline is reasonable on one scan before you batch-process three hundred.
Plotting is optional because matplotlib is heavy and this library is pure numpy by default. pip install dpv-monopeak[plot] pulls it in. The core stays at one dependency.

title: dpv-monopeak
text:
Testing against synthetic peaks
The test suite generates Gaussian peaks on flat and tilted baselines and checks the extracted features against analytic ground truth, to within discretization error. Peak voltage within one sample step, height within one percent, FWHM within two sample steps, area within five percent. Off-center peaks, edge peaks, linear baselines. The left-chop heuristic is tested for correctness and for pluggability: inject a recording lambda and confirm it was called exactly once with the right peak index.
Every edge case that returns None has a test. Peak at the last sample, flat current, mismatched array lengths. If a scan should fail, the test asserts it does.

title: dpv-monopeak
text:
dpv-calibration
There is a sibling package, dpv-calibration, that turns these eight features into concentration-response curves. Point it at a directory of scans from known concentrations, it extracts features from each, fits a model, and returns calibration parameters. It is less mature, currently in that awkward phase where the API surface is mapped out but the edge cases are still being found by throwing real data at it. It exists because once feature extraction is clean, calibration is the obvious next thing, and bundling both into one package felt wrong. Feature extraction is a solved problem here. Calibration is a modeling problem with its own failure modes.

title: dpv-monopeak
text:
What I got wrong
The monopeak assumption is baked into the package name and every function signature. Right call for the instrument it was built for. It also means that if someone hands you a scan with two Faradaic peaks, the library quietly picks the taller one and pretends the other is not there. A validate_monopeak check that scans the corrected current for secondary peaks above some fraction of the main Height would catch it. I skipped it because every scan I had seen from our instrument was single-peak. The first time I ran it on a different dataset, that assumption broke.
The other miss is error reporting. Returning None from every failure path is clean code and terrible debugging. When a batch job runs 200 scans and 14 silently drop, you have no idea why until you re-run those 14 through compute_dpv and stare at the intermediates. A reason key next to the None would have saved me an afternoon.

title: Syringe Pump Automation
text:
We run experiments that need three syringe pumps moving at once: one Harvard Apparatus Pump 11 Elite and two New Era NE-4002X pumps daisy-chained on a single RS-232 line. The Harvard speaks one serial protocol. The New Eras speak another, with address prefixes for the daisy chain. Neither has a Python driver that validates rates properly. Both will happily accept an out-of-range command and either reject it at the firmware level with a useless error code or, worse, run at some rate you did not ask for.
This software wraps both pump types behind one PumpController API, with hardware-level rate and volume validation that runs before any serial command reaches the pump. It ships a tkinter UI with three tabs (setup, manual control, script orchestration) and a run.bat launcher that makes the whole thing double-clickable on Windows.

title: Syringe Pump Automation
section: Rate limits as a feature, not a guardrail
text:
Rate limits as a feature, not a guardrail
The key decision is that rate validation is not a safety net. It is the primary interface. Every infuse and withdraw call checks the requested rate against the pump’s mechanical limits at the given syringe diameter before it builds the serial command. Out of range, it raises RateOutOfRange with the exact allowed range in the message. The command never reaches the port.
This matters because the two pump types have wildly different limits at the same diameter. Take a typical 12 mm syringe. The Harvard can push up to 18.3 mL per minute. The New Era NE-4002X, a microfluidic pump, tops out at 0.249 mL per minute at the same diameter, about seventy times slower. Write a protocol that assumes both pumps handle 1 mL per minute and the Harvard is fine while the New Era rejects it. Validation catches that before the experiment starts, not thirty seconds into a dispense when one pump has already moved.
The limits are diameter-dependent because flow rate is pusher velocity times syringe cross-sectional area. The Harvard’s pusher travels from 0.000153 to 159.0 millimeters per minute. The New Era’s limits come from a per-diameter table in the spec sheet, interpolated between listed values and clamped to an absolute ceiling of 1226 microliters per minute. Every number in pump_limits.py is back-solved from the manufacturer documentation and checked against hardware. The docstrings cite the source document and appendix.

title: Syringe Pump Automation
text:
Volume caps
The Harvard has no hard ceiling on a single dispense. The New Era firmware uses a four-digit microliter field, which caps a single dispense at 9999 microliters, roughly 10 mL. Ask for more and it raises VolumeOutOfRange. The workaround is continuous mode (set volume to zero and time the run yourself) or a loop of smaller dispenses. The error message says which. It does not just refuse and leave you guessing.

title: Syringe Pump Automation
text:
Per-pump worker threads
Each registered pump gets its own PumpWorker thread with a task queue. Setup commands (diameter, rate, volume) are queued as callables and run sequentially in the worker. The main thread stays responsive, which matters in the UI, where a frozen window looks exactly like a crashed program.
The workers are plain threading.Thread instances with daemon set to False. They run until a sentinel None task arrives or a stop event is set. Errors collect in a per-worker list rather than raising in the calling thread, so a setup failure on pump B does not stop pump C from initializing. The UI polls the error lists and surfaces failures per pump.
The daisy-chained New Eras share one serial port. The NewEraNetwork class owns the port and each NewEraPump holds a reference to it plus an address. A lock on the network keeps two pumps from talking over each other on the shared bus. The Harvard gets its own COM port and never contends for anything.

title: Syringe Pump Automation
text:
The UI
Three tabs. Setup configures and connects each pump one at a time: type, port, address, and a Connect button that turns green when the pump answers. Manual runs one or more pumps right now with fixed settings: diameter, rate, volume, direction, Run. Orchestrate is a text editor with a Run Script button.
Orchestrate is where it gets interesting. Paste a Python script straight into the editor, or hit Load to open one from protocols/, or Insert Template for a skeleton, or LLM Prompt to copy the full API context to your clipboard so you can drop it into any model and have it write the protocol for you. The generated script goes back in the editor. Run Script releases the UI’s COM port connections, spawns the script as a subprocess, streams its stdout into the log pane, and reconnects the pumps when it finishes.
The STOP ALL button at the bottom kills any running subprocess, reconnects the pumps, and sends a stop to every registered pump. It is the emergency brake, so you never have to find the terminal window, dig up a PID, and kill it by hand.

title: Syringe Pump Automation
text:
The script API
Scripts use the same PumpController as the UI, so there is no second interface to learn. A script opens its own controller and COM ports, runs the experiment, and closes everything in a finally block. The template includes a Ctrl+C handler that calls stop_all and close_all before exiting, so an interrupted script leaves the pumps stopped instead of free-running.
from pump_controller import PumpController

ctrl = PumpController(log_file='logs/experiment.log')
ctrl.add_harvard('pump_a', port='COM6')
ctrl.add_new_era('pump_b', port='COM7', address=0)

ctrl.run_parallel([
    {'pump_id': 'pump_a', 'rate': 1.0, 'units': 'ml/min',
     'volume': 2.0, 'diameter_mm': 14.43, 'direction': 'infuse'},
    {'pump_id': 'pump_b', 'rate': 0.2, 'units': 'ml/hr',
     'volume': 0.5, 'diameter_mm': 8.58, 'direction': 'withdraw'},
])
ctrl.close_all()
run_parallel blocks until every pump in the list finishes. infuse and withdraw on a single pump block too. That is intentional. The API is synchronous because async pump control adds complexity without buying anything for this use case. Need two pumps moving together? Use run_parallel. Need them in sequence? Call infuse then withdraw on separate lines. There is no event loop to reason about.

title: Syringe Pump Automation
section: LLM integration as a deliberate side channel
text:
LLM integration as a deliberate side channel
The LLM Prompt button does not call an API. It opens a popup with a text block: the full hardware configuration, the syringe diameter reference table, the rate limit tables, the API reference, and the generation rules. You copy it, paste it into ChatGPT or Claude, and describe your experiment in plain English. The model writes a complete script with the right diameters, rate limits, and error handling. You paste the result back into the editor.
This is deliberately low-tech. Embedding an LLM call would add an API key, a network round trip, and a failure mode I cannot reproduce. Copy-paste keeps the model as a tool the researcher uses, not a dependency the software carries. If the model is down, you still have the template and the API reference. If the model writes bad code, you read it before you run it. There is no black box between you and the motor.
The prompt text lives in llms.txt at the project root, so it doubles as documentation for any human who wants the full API surface in one file.

title: Syringe Pump Automation
text:
What I got wrong
The original protocol assumed both pump types could handle milliliter-per-minute rates. Wrong by a factor of forty for the New Era at a typical diameter. I found out when the hardware rejected a rate and handed back a firmware error code with no explanation. The fix was pump_limits.py, which back-solves every limit from the manufacturer docs and checks the table entries against real hardware responses. That table is now the single source of truth for what any pump can do at any diameter.
Then there was the volume convention. PumpController takes milliliters, the New Era firmware speaks microliters, and the driver converts internally. I did not document that clearly at first, so a script asked for 0.001 mL thinking it meant 1 microliter and got exactly that. Correct, and confusing, because the log showed a number that did not match the mental model. The convention is now stated in every code example and in llms.txt.
I would also redo the worker thread model. As it stands, tasks queue per pump and there is no way to wait for all setup across all pumps to finish before starting. The UI papers over this with status polling, but a script that calls add_harvard and then infuse immediately can race the setup. A wait_until_ready that blocks until every worker has drained its queue would close the gap.

title: Credit Risk Modeling with SVMs
text:
Credit card default prediction is a classification problem with a twist: the two kinds of error are not equally bad. Miss a client who is about to default (false negative) and the bank loses money. Flag a client who is actually fine (false positive) and you get a declined transaction, which is annoying but recoverable.
Standard classifiers do not know this. They minimize overall error, which on an imbalanced dataset mostly means learning to predict the majority class and ignoring the minority. Here we use kernel SVMs to build a credit risk model and handle that asymmetry on purpose.
Dataset: UCI Default of Credit Card Clients. 30,000 clients, 23 features (payment history, bill amounts, demographics), binary target (does the client default next month). No missing values, no preprocessing headaches.

title: Credit Risk Modeling with SVMs
text:
Credit card default prediction is a classification problem with a twist: the two kinds of error are not equally bad. Miss a client who is about to default (false negative) and the bank loses money. Flag a client who is actually fine (false positive) and you get a declined transaction, which is annoying but recoverable.
Standard classifiers do not know this. They minimize overall error, which on an imbalanced dataset mostly means learning to predict the majority class and ignoring the minority. Here we use kernel SVMs to build a credit risk model and handle that asymmetry on purpose.
Dataset: UCI Default of Credit Card Clients. 30,000 clients, 23 features (payment history, bill amounts, demographics), binary target (does the client default next month). No missing values, no preprocessing headaches.

title: Credit Risk Modeling with SVMs
text:
Data split
The test set is held out immediately and not touched until the final evaluation. Inside the training set, we carve out a validation set for every hyperparameter decision. Normalization is fit on train_train only and applied forward to val and test, so nothing downstream leaks back into the fit.

from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

scaler_X = StandardScaler()

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=42)
X_train_train, X_train_val, y_train_train, y_train_val = train_test_split(X_train, y_train, test_size=0.2, random_state=42)

scaler_X.fit(X_train_train)
X_train_train_scaled = scaler_X.transform(X_train_train)
X_train_val_scaled   = scaler_X.transform(X_train_val)
X_test_scaled        = scaler_X.transform(X_test)

print(f'train_train: {len(X_train_train_scaled)}')
print(f'train_val:   {len(X_train_val_scaled)}')
print(f'test:        {len(X_test_scaled)}')

x_train_train_scaled 16800
x_train_val_scaled 4200
x_test_scaled 9000

title: Credit Risk Modeling with SVMs
text:
Base RBF SVC
RBF SVM is the natural starting point for tabular classification. The kernel \(K(x_i, x_j) = \exp(-\gamma \|x_i - x_j\|^2)\) maps the data into a high-dimensional space where a linear separator often exists even when the original feature space is not linearly separable.
Before tuning anything, look at what the default model actually learned. The SVM dual problem is:
\[\max_{\alpha} \sum_i \alpha_i - \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i,j} \alpha_i \alpha_j y_i y_j K(x_i, x_j)\]
subject to \(0 \leq \alpha_i \leq C\) and \(\sum_i \alpha_i y_i = 0\). Points with \(\alpha_i > 0\) are support vectors, the only training points that matter at inference time. Prediction for a new point \(x\) is:
\[f(x) = \sum_{i \in SV} \alpha_i y_i K(x_i, x) + b\]

from sklearn import svm

rbf_svc = svm.SVC(kernel='rbf', probability=True).fit(X_train_train_scaled, y_train_train)

print('Support vectors per class:', rbf_svc.n_support_)
print('dual_coef_ shape:         ', rbf_svc.dual_coef_.shape)

Support vectors per class: [4150 3262]
dual_coef_ shape:          (1, 7412)


7,412 support vectors out of 16,800 training points, about 44%. That is high, and it tells us the default decision boundary is not clean. The classes overlap a lot in feature space, so the model needs many points to pin down the margin.
dual_coef_ has shape (1, 7412), one \(\alpha_i y_i\) per support vector. Large magnitude means that support vector is pulling hard on the boundary. Most cluster near the margin. The high-magnitude ones are the contested, borderline clients.

title: Credit Risk Modeling with SVMs
text:
Hyperparameter tuning
Two knobs matter for the RBF SVM:

C: penalty for margin violations. Low C gives a wider, softer margin. High C fits tighter and risks overfitting.
gamma: kernel bandwidth. Low gamma means each point influences a wide region and the boundary is smooth. High gamma makes influence local, the boundary complex, the support vector count high, and memorization likely.

We sweep a grid and track both validation F1 and support vector count.

from sklearn.svm import SVC
from sklearn.metrics import f1_score

title: Credit Risk Modeling with SVMs
text:
Asymmetric margins
The baseline model at C=1, gamma=0.1 has recall of 0.36 on the default class. It is missing 64% of actual defaulters. For a bank, that is the worst failure mode there is.
A standard SVM penalizes both classes equally. We fix that with separate penalty parameters \(C^+\) and \(C^-\) in the primal:
\[\min_{w,b,\xi} \frac{1}{2}\|w\|^2 + C^+ \sum_{i: y_i=1} \xi_i + C^- \sum_{i: y_i=-1} \xi_i\]
Setting \(C^+ > C^-\) makes misclassifying a defaulter more expensive. The boundary shifts away from the positive class to give it more margin, trading precision for recall on the class that actually matters.
We try three setups: baseline (no weighting), balanced (auto-computed from class frequencies), and manual ({0:1, 1:5}).

from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix, classification_report

baseline.fit(X_train_train_scaled, y_train_train)
y_pred_base = baseline.predict(X_train_val_scaled)

balanced = svm.SVC(kernel='rbf', gamma=best_gamma, C=best_C, class_weight='balanced', probability=True)
balanced.fit(X_train_train_scaled, y_train_train)
y_pred_bal = balanced.predict(X_train_val_scaled)

manual = svm.SVC(kernel='rbf', gamma=best_gamma, C=best_C, class_weight={0:1, 1:5}, probability=True)
manual.fit(X_train_train_scaled, y_train_train)
y_pred_man = manual.predict(X_train_val_scaled)

title: Credit Risk Modeling with SVMs
text:
Probability scoring via Platt scaling
Hard class labels are usually not what you want in credit risk. A probability of default is more useful, because it lets you rank applicants, set thresholds, and feed downstream risk systems.
Setting probability=True enables Platt scaling. After the SVM trains, a logistic regression is fit with 5-fold internal CV to map the decision function \(f(x)\) to a probability:
\[P(y=1 \mid x) = \frac{1}{1 + \exp(A \cdot f(x) + B)}\]
where \(A\) and \(B\) are fit by MLE. The decision function measures signed distance to the hyperplane: large positive means the model is confident the client defaults, large negative means confident they will not. Platt scaling turns that distance into a calibrated probability.
The internal CV is what keeps this honest. It stops the calibration from just memorizing training labels. What comes out is a score you can actually read: predict_proba(x)[1] reflects the empirical default rate among clients with similar features.

title: A transformer walks into a compression problem
text:
Lossless compression is probability modeling. Full stop.
If you can predict the next symbol, you can encode it efficiently. The better the prediction, the shorter the code. The theoretical floor is the entropy of the source, and everything above that floor is the gap between your model and the true distribution.
The question is whether a transformer can close that gap without ever being told what distribution the data came from. No parameters, no prior, no generative story. Just a sequence of bits and a model that has to figure out what comes next.
I built a research platform to answer this. Binary sequences only, because binary is where you can compare against closed-form optimal estimators and know exactly how far from the bound you are. The transformer is small, 3 layers, 3 attention heads, roughly 90K parameters. It is trained offline on sequences from some source and then evaluated at test time one bit at a time, same as any classical estimator.
The results are honestly not too bad.

title: A transformer walks into a compression problem
section: The general transformer learns Laplace from data
text:
The general transformer learns Laplace from data
Start with IID Bernoulli sequences. Flip a biased coin with unknown probability p and generate sequences of length N. The transformer has never seen this p, it was trained on sequences with p drawn uniformly from (0, 1).
At test time the model sees a sequence and predicts P(next bit = 1) at each step. Its baseline is the Laplace estimator, which counts the number of 1s seen so far and computes (k+1)/(t+2). Laplace is near-optimal for IID data and requires zero training.
Across every p we tested (0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9) and every sequence length from N=10 to N=499, the transformer tracks Laplace almost exactly. At N=10 the gap is around 0.16 BPS. By N=499 the gap collapses to roughly 0.007 BPS.
This makes sense because there is no temporal structure for the transformer to exploit. The IID source has no memory. What the transformer learns is the inference rule itself: count, add pseudocounts, normalize. It learns to approximate the Bayes-optimal estimator from data alone, without ever being told the prior.

title: A transformer walks into a compression problem
section: Specialized training gives you a prior
text:
Specialized training gives you a prior
The general model does fine, but it starts every test sequence from square one. It has no information about which p is more likely, because it was trained on a uniform distribution over p.
What happens if you train a transformer on sequences from a single p? Now the model has seen 10,000 sequences all drawn from p=0.3. It knows, in its weights, that p is probably around 0.3.
At N=10 this matters a lot. The specialized transformer hits 0.910 BPS while Laplace sits at 0.976. That 0.066 gap is the value of knowing the source distribution in advance. As sequences grow longer the gap shrinks, because the data overwhelms the prior. By N=499 the gap is 0.007.
This is exactly what you would expect from Bayesian inference. The prior dominates when data is scarce. The likelihood dominates when data is abundant. The transformer learned the prior from its training distribution and uses it at test time the same way a Bayesian estimator would.

title: A transformer walks into a compression problem
text:
Redundancy scales as 1/m
The Høst-Madsen bound says the redundancy, which is the gap between the model’s BPS and the source entropy, should decay roughly as 1/m where m is the number of training sequences. I tested this by training transformers on m = 10, 25, 50, 75, 100, 150, 200, 300, 500, 1000 sequences and measuring BPS at test length N=100.
The data matches the bound. On a log-log plot the redundancy drops cleanly with a slope near -1. The crossover point where the transformer beats Laplace is around m=100 training sequences. At m=50 the transformer redundancy is 0.040 BPS above entropy, at m=100 it is 0.021, at m=1000 it drops to 0.005.
This is not surprising if you believe the bound, but it is satisfying to see a small transformer hit it. The thing has 90K parameters and was trained for 500 iterations per checkpoint. It is not doing anything exotic. It is just learning the counting rule from repeated exposure, and the efficiency of that learning follows the same scaling law as the optimal estimator.

title: A transformer walks into a compression problem
section: Markov and FSM: structure is where the money is
text:
Markov and FSM: structure is where the money is
IID is the baseline. The interesting part is structured sources.
On the binary symmetric Markov chain the specialized transformer dominates. At p_stay=0.99, where the chain almost never flips, the specialized model hits 0.317 BPS at N=499 while Laplace sits at 0.789 and the general IID transformer at 0.809. CTW eventually catches up (0.317 as well at N=499) but it takes context to get there, at N=10 CTW is stuck at 1.0 because it has not seen enough symbols to fill its context window. The transformer starts strong immediately.
The setup is symmetric: the specialized model was trained on Markov chains with the same p_stay, the IID transformer was trained on IID sequences, and CTW builds a context tree online. The IID transformer does pick up some in-context adaptation on Markov (it tracks the transitions), but the gains are small. What actually beats CTW is knowing the source in advance through specialized training.
On a deterministic 4-state FSM the pattern holds. Specialized transformer leads at every sequence length. N=10: transformer 0.760 BPS, CTW 1.000. N=499: transformer 0.746, CTW 0.798, Laplace 0.810. The ~0.05 BPS gap at long sequences is the transformer’s offline knowledge paying off.
On Dirichlet-Markov sources with random transition matrices the specialized transformer beats Laplace and CTW at every alpha tested. The advantage widens as alpha increases (more concentrated priors, less entropy in the transition structure).

title: A transformer walks into a compression problem
text:
Where the counting lives
The cleanest result is from probing the attention heads. The Bayes-optimal estimate for IID data under a Beta(α, β) prior is (k+α)/(t+α+β). This is a linear function of two counts: the number of 1s seen (k) and the total symbols seen (t). So you can fit a linear probe to the transformer’s attention outputs at each layer and check whether the model has computed this quantity.
It has. For a transformer trained under Beta(5,2), the probe achieves R²=0.82 at Layer 0. For most models Layer 0 dominates, meaning the counting and prior correction happens in the first attention layer. The raw k/t probe, which just checks whether the model is counting without the prior correction, scores lower at every layer for every model.
What this shows is that the prior correction is in the attention weights, not deferred to the MLP later. The model is doing something structurally Bayesian: count the observations in attention, apply the prior correction in the same operation, output the probability. The R² scales with prior concentration too, Beta(0.5,0.5) peaks at 0.43 while Beta(5,2) reaches 0.82, which makes sense because a concentrated prior produces sharper predictions that are easier to read out linearly.
I did not expect the probe to work this cleanly. A 3-layer transformer with 90K parameters learning a closed-form Bayesian estimator from scratch, and you can literally read the estimate off the first layer’s attention outputs with a linear regression. That is satisfying in a way that most ML results are not.
